{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=autonomous+system+objective+synthesis+from+ambient+feedback+mechanisms&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6738378\", \"title\": [\"From Monitoring to Control: A Feedback-Driven Autonomous System for API Workflow Reliability\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Traditional API monitoring systems emphasize observability through anomaly detection and alerting, but fall short in ensuring reliable execution of distributed workflows involving interdependent services, partial failures, and irreversible actions. This paper introduces a novel control-driven paradigm that reframes API monitoring as a closed-loop feedback system for maintaining workflow correctness. Drawing from control theory, we propose a feedback-driven autonomous framework that continuously observes system telemetry, evaluates workflow state consistency, and applies adaptive control actions to mitigate deviations from expected behavior. Unlike existing approaches based on static synthetic tests or reactive anomaly detection, the proposed method models API workflows as dynamic stateful processes and enforces reliability through continuous correction and stabilization. The framework is evaluated using a simulated multi-step transactional system with injected failure scenarios, demonstrating significant improvements in mean time to recovery (MTTR), workflow consistency, and failure resolution effectiveness. La première loi de commande a été conçue en utilisant une technique de type backstepping et une preuve de stabilité exponentielle locale a été obtenue. La deuxième loi de commande utilise une approche de type commande prédictive non linéaire (CPNL). L'objectif de commande consiste alors à minimiser une fonction coût en tenant compte des contraintes sur les actionneurs. actions.body: Analysis of existing cognitive architectures (source-bda2bc47c38c47a2) reveals a persistent reliance on predefined control loops and human-in-the-loop validation. Recent work focusing on evolving AI agents (source-db145486024f469a, source-f955850b0fcf467a) suggests that while autonomy is expanding, rigorous self-correction—defined as the capacity for an architecture to autonomously detect and rectify its own internal reasoning errors—remains largely externalized. These architectures often delegate error correction to alignment or monitoring layers rather than embedding them as fundamental architectural properties. Consequently, current research requires a shift in focus from static architectural categorization toward dynamic, autonomous error-monitoring frameworks.
